definitions.meaning: the head of a convent is addressed as Mother followed by this title
the largest of North America's Great Lakes bears this name after the word Lake

explanation.walkthrough: Each clue word is a name that the answer completes: the convent head and the Great Lake share the same second word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means higher-ranking, which gives a convent's head her title and also names the uppermost of the Great Lakes.

parts.note: a cheerful (gay) writer would never produce tearful, sentimental writing

explanation.walkthrough: Gay looks like the poet John Gay, but here it means merry: weepy sentimental material is no work of a cheerful person.
explanation.definitionFit: Mawkish writing designed to make people cry is sentimental material, the opposite of cheerful.

clue.text: Open house at the Inns of Court ?

definitions.text: Open house at the Inns of Court ?

parts.words: Open house at the Inns of Court ?
parts.note: the Inns of Court are where barristers are trained and called to the bar; a pub room open to all is a bar too

explanation.walkthrough: The Inns of Court are the London societies of barristers, 'the Bar'; a pub's plainer drinking room, open to anyone, is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The ordinary drinking room of a British pub, open to everyone, a counter for the general populace.

definitions.meaning: small individual loaves or buns
turns over and over, revolves

explanation.surface: A loaf is passed around the table.
explanation.definitionFit: Small baked loaves are known by this plural noun, and the verb means turns or revolves.

indicators.note: the abbreviation for anagram tells the solver to rearrange the letters of the expression

parts.note: the symbols are spoken as two O letters with the subtraction word between them

explanation.surface: A bare scoreline of nil to nil looks menacing.
explanation.walkthrough: Read '0-O' aloud as 'O minus O'; those seven letters rearranged give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that portends trouble is menacing or threatening.

definitions.meaning: telephoned someone
to go one step higher, up a single crossbar of a ladder

explanation.surface: Someone is summoned and told to climb a ladder.
explanation.definitionFit: To phone someone is an idiom meaning telephoned, and read literally it is going up one crossbar of a ladder.

definitions.meaning: a formal occasion when a statue or plaque is first shown
a nun leaving would take off her veil

explanation.walkthrough: A nun wears a veil; leaving the convent she removes it, which is also the name of a ceremony revealing a monument.
explanation.definitionFit: Formally revealing a plaque or statue by removing its cover is an occasion, and a departing nun removes her headcovering.

clue.text: He often came for a rubber

definitions.text: He often came for a rubber

parts.words: He often came for a rubber
parts.note: in the Aladdin story rubbing the lamp summons a spirit; a rubber is not an eraser but a person rubbing

explanation.walkthrough: A rubber looks like an eraser or a game of bridge, but here it is one who rubs, like Aladdin with his lamp.
explanation.definitionFit: The spirit of the lamp in the Arabian Nights appears whenever the lamp is rubbed.

indicators.note: spoken out loud the word for requests sounds like the answer

parts.note: pleas are earnest requests or appeals

explanation.surface: Someone tries to satisfy appeals once they have been listened to.
explanation.definitionFit: To give pleasure or satisfaction is to gratify someone.

annotationWithheld.why: 'Thy cat Gabby' (6): the wordplay is an anagram of THY CAT but no clue word signals the anagram, so the op has no indicator

parts.note: Bob is a short form of Robert, as is Robbie, so Robbie's gives Bob's
Aurora Leigh is the heroine of Elizabeth Barrett Browning's verse novel, so Aurora calls up her surname

explanation.surface: Robbie looks sleek and slippery in the company of a girl called Aurora.
explanation.walkthrough: Aurora is not the dawn or the northern lights here but Aurora Leigh, the title character of Elizabeth Barrett Browning's long poem.
explanation.definitionFit: A racing sled on an ice run, a vehicle that is all about sliding fast.

clue.text: A this could be a shady way to meet

definitions.text: A this could be a shady way to meet

parts.words: A this could be a shady way to meet
parts.note: put A before the answer and you get a tree-lined road, a shady way; on its own the word is a meeting place

explanation.walkthrough: The clue works in two halves: 'A this' means the letter A followed by the answer, giving a tree-lined road, and 'to meet' points to a place where people gather.
explanation.definitionFit: A venue is a place where an event or meeting is held, a meeting place.

definitions.meaning: understands, catches on to, in informal British speech
small thin branches of a tree

explanation.surface: Someone clutches at flimsy pieces of wood.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally it means understands, and as a plural noun it means slender shoots or branches.

definitions.meaning: rank ..., people beyond the pale of decent society
the knifeboard was the long back-to-back bench on the roof of a horse-drawn omnibus, where passengers rode outside

explanation.surface: Disreputable men are riding on top of a Victorian bus.
explanation.walkthrough: A knifeboard was the bench running along the roof of an old London omnibus; people riding up there, not inside, were called by the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Socially unacceptable people are those excluded from the circle, and bus-roof passengers sat on the exterior.

definitions.meaning: cloths or textiles
a headquarters for the Football Association would be built with FA bricks, which sounds like the answer

explanation.surface: Someone is ordering supplies to build the headquarters of English football.
explanation.walkthrough: FA is the Football Association, English football's governing body; bricks for its headquarters would be 'FA bricks'.
explanation.definitionFit: Woven cloths and textiles are all kinds of material.

clue.text: Site of the abbey hospital in Somerset ?

definitions.text: Site of the abbey hospital in Somerset ?

parts.words: Site of the abbey hospital in Somerset ?
parts.note: an abbey church is a minster, and a hospital is where the ill go; an ill minster would be an abbey hospital

explanation.walkthrough: The Somerset market town sounds like 'ill minster', a sick abbey church, read as an abbey hospital.
explanation.definitionFit: A market town in Somerset, England, named after its minster church.

parts.note: the chase is a fox hunt, and this is the cry huntsmen shout to urge on the hounds

explanation.definitionFit: This is a traditional fox-hunting cry used to encourage the hounds.

parts.note: in the Book of Ruth Boaz is a relative of Naomi's dead husband, so she was a female relation of his

explanation.walkthrough: In the Old Testament Book of Ruth, Boaz is a kinsman of Naomi's husband Elimelech, so Naomi was his relation by marriage.
explanation.definitionFit: A female relative by blood or marriage, as Naomi was to her husband's clansman.

clue.text: Winds around, but pedals round no turning

indicators.note: the word for pedals is placed round the reversed word

parts.note: pedalling a bicycle is cycling, so pedals gives cycles

indicators.note: turning means the word no is read backwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone cycles round in circles without ever turning off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Winds' reads as a verb, coiling round, but it is the plural noun for storms of air.
explanation.definitionFit: Storms of air rotating about a low-pressure centre are winds that go round.

definitions.meaning: of poor quality, rubbishy, in informal speech
3-down is bread buns, whose leftovers are crumbs; covered in those, something would be described by the answer

explanation.surface: Something is as useless as the leftovers of bread.
explanation.walkthrough: The '3' refers to the answer at 3-down, bread buns; their remnants are crumbs, and something full of crumbs is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally the word means shoddy or worthless, and literally it means full of crumbs.

clue.text: Loud in a campus the call of a bird

indicators.note: the musical marking goes inside the university's name

parts.note: Yale is an American university campus
ff, fortissimo, is the musical marking for very loud

explanation.surface: A bird's loud cry rings out across a university campus.
explanation.walkthrough: Yale is an American Ivy League university; FF, fortissimo, is the musical marking for very loud.
explanation.definitionFit: This dialect name for the green woodpecker imitates its laughing cry.

clue.text: Force of an old boat taking ye back round North Carolina

parts.note: a cog was a broad medieval sailing ship

indicators.note: the reversed word goes round the state abbreviation, enclosing it
taking the word ye back means writing it in reverse order

parts.note: taken as written
NC is the postal abbreviation for the US state

explanation.surface: An old ship sails home carrying its crew around the coast of North Carolina.
explanation.walkthrough: A cog was a broad-beamed sailing ship of the Middle Ages, so 'old boat' points to it.
explanation.definitionFit: Persuasive power or strength of argument is a kind of force.

definitions.meaning: a capital city, here that of Ceylon
the chief port of Ceylon, the great tea-growing island, from which tea is shipped

explanation.surface: A splendid spot to stop for a cup of tea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' seems to mean splendid, but it is a capital city: that of Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, famous for tea.
explanation.definitionFit: This port was the capital of Ceylon, the island famous for growing tea.

parts.note: Beau is said like bow; a dandy (beau) of Regency days wore a broad neckcloth

explanation.walkthrough: 'Beau tie' sounds like bow tie, but a beau is a dandy like Beau Brummell, famous for his neckcloth.
explanation.definitionFit: A wide scarf knotted at the throat, the neckwear of a Regency dandy.

clue.text: Nurse left in a tizzy and high dudgeon

definitions.note: a noun phrase standing for the adjective, read as 'in high dudgeon', with 'in' carried over from the indicator

indicators.note: a tizzy is a state of nervous confusion, so these letters are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: A nurse has stormed out, flustered and angry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a tizzy' scrambles the nine letters of NURSE LEFT.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone in high dudgeon is deeply offended and indignant, bitterly aggrieved.

clue.text: Dished by some salt on the motorway

definitions.note: a past participle standing for a noun: the answer is a dish, the clue says something dished up

indicators.note: only some of the word salt is taken, its opening letters

parts.note: the M1, Britain's first motorway, written with I for 1

explanation.surface: Food served by someone who put salt on it on the motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is Britain's first motorway, from London to Yorkshire; its 1 is read as I.
explanation.definitionFit: A salmi is a ragout of game birds, a dish served at table.

clue.text: One way to beat the wet

definitions.text: One way to beat the wet

parts.words: One way to beat the wet
parts.note: drying yourself off with a cloth after a bath or swim is a way of defeating wetness

explanation.definitionFit: This absorbent cloth is used for drying the body, so it overcomes being wet.

parts.note: gas used to be billed by a unit of heat, so the gas supply is personified as the unit it is sold in

explanation.walkthrough: British gas bills used to be reckoned in a unit of heat equal to 100,000 British thermal units.
explanation.definitionFit: A unit of heat formerly used to measure and charge for gas supply.

parts.note: vale is Latin for goodbye

indicators.note: the second word is taken without the letter that 'no' supplies

parts.note: taken as written
no is nought, the letter O

explanation.surface: Someone says goodbye to the famous butler, no less.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no less' reads as 'O less', taking the O out; Jeeves is P. G. Wodehouse's gentleman's gentleman.
explanation.definitionFit: Jeeves is the personal manservant to Bertie Wooster in Wodehouse's stories, an example of a gentleman's gentleman.

definitions.meaning: people who store lumber, i.e. unwanted junk such as white elephants
men who fell trees for timber

explanation.surface: A group of men look after useless old possessions.
explanation.walkthrough: A white elephant is a costly, unwanted possession; such junk is called lumber, so its hoarders are lumber men.
explanation.definitionFit: Lumber means both stored junk and timber, so the word covers men who keep junk and men who cut down trees.

definitions.note: read as 'statesman-like', a statesman's name: a noun is wanted, the setter attaching 'like' to say the anagram resembles him

indicators.note: the word Theirs once was, before its letters were rearranged, so it signals a change of order

explanation.surface: A group of people behaved like politicians of stature.
explanation.walkthrough: Adolphe Thiers was the French statesman who became first President of the Third Republic; his name is the clue's first word with two letters swapped.
explanation.definitionFit: Thiers was a leading nineteenth-century French politician and President of France.

parts.note: Herrick's poem 'To Anthea, who may command him anything' makes her orders ones the poet could not refuse

explanation.walkthrough: Robert Herrick wrote 'To Anthea, who may command him anything', promising to obey whatever she bade.
explanation.definitionFit: Orders that must be obeyed are what a lover could never refuse.
